body:
# The canonical register: Skr

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Skr, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Skr to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𓋴𓎡𓂋𓅃**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Skr**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “SOH-kar” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *sokar* is *not false — it is a fallback*, and the register is exact about what that means. In systems that cannot carry diacritics (legacy databases, older tooling, parts of the address-bar pipeline) the flattened form is the accepted vehicle, and the rulebook names it explicitly as the final rung of the fallback hierarchy: full restoration first, circumflex where attested, macron-only by the academic standard, an attested variant, and only then plain ASCII.

What the fallback status forbids is promotion: *sokar* may carry the name where marks are impossible, but it may not *represent* the name where marks are possible.  A fallback is a vehicle, never the primary.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Sokar is a study in controlled fusion: with Ptah as Ptah-Sokar, with Osiris as Sokar-Osiris, and in the full Memphite formula as all three.  The Greeks rendered him Sarapis’ deepest Egyptian stratum — the Apis bull’s Memphite necropolis was Sokar’s ground long before Serapis was imagined.

And it never stopped working. His festival ship, the Henu, survives in hundreds of amulets and in the standard late coffin-foot vignette; and the Djed-raising rite he hosted became the emblematic ‘erection of Osiris’ celebrated at the New Year across Egypt.  The Memphite trinity remains the textbook example of Egyptian god-compounding done to completion.

## The Convention's Own History

Egyptological transliteration exists because hieroglyphs write consonants, not vowels. The characters ꜣ (aleph) and ꜥ (ayin) are consonants — a glottal reed and a pharyngeal grip — and rendering them as vowels does not "simplify" the name, it deletes consonants from it. The conventions in use descend from nineteenth-century decipherment and the standardized Manuel de Codage: ḥ, ḫ, ḏ, ṯ each mark a distinct consonant the Egyptian wrote and a modern reader must not merge. When this register defends them, it defends the principle that a writing system older than the alphabet gets to keep its consonants.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Skr** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Skr** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *sokar* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Skr** stands at [/sokar/](/sokar/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Memphite funerary liturgies and the Shabaka Stone tradition, Sokar-festival reliefs and Henu-barque iconography, Deir el-Medina ostraca (craft invocations).
